start: Of all the means which are procured by wisdom
context: Epicurus lived with his friends in a community called the Garden. For him, friendship was not an extra in a good life but its foundation.
prompt: Which friendship deserves more of your attention than it has been getting?

start: Death, therefore, the most awful of evils
end: death is come, we are not.
context: Epicurus wanted to free people from the fear of death, which he saw as poisoning ordinary life. Where we are, death is not; where death is, we are not.
prompt: If fear of an ending were set aside, how would you spend this day?

start: Let no one be slow to seek wisdom
context: The opening of Epicurus' letter summarising his ethics. Philosophy, for him, was a lifelong practice of caring for the soul, never too early and never too late.
prompt: What are you still curious to learn about how to live?

start: Nature’s wealth at once has its bounds
context: Natural needs are few and easily met. Desires born of imagination keep moving out of reach however much we acquire.
prompt: Which of your wants keeps receding the closer you get?

source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things II
start: 'Tis sweet, when, down the mighty main
context: Lucretius, a Roman poet, set Epicurus' philosophy to verse. Here he describes the calm of a mind that has found its footing, looking out on a restless world.
prompt: Where is your 'serene plateau' when life gets stormy?

start: Accustom thyself to believe that death is nothing to us
context: The goal is not to make life longer but to make mortal life enjoyable, by letting go of the craving to live forever.
prompt: How would you live if you made peace with being mortal?

start: And even as men choose of food
context: The quality of a life matters more than its length, just as we choose food for its taste, not its quantity.
prompt: How could you make today sweeter rather than longer?

start: We must remember that the future is neither wholly ours
context: A balanced stance toward the future: neither counting on it nor despairing of it.
prompt: What are you either counting on or despairing of too much?

start: For the end of all our actions is to be free from pain and fear
end: tempest of the soul is laid
context: Epicurus' aim was ataraxia, a calm, untroubled mind. Once it is reached, there is nothing more to chase.
prompt: What is stirring a tempest in your soul right now?

start: we do not choose every pleasure whatsoever
end: brings us as a consequence a greater pleasure.
context: Epicurus is often mistaken for a hedonist. In fact he taught careful weighing: some pleasures cost too much, some pains are worth it.
prompt: Which pleasure costs you more than it gives?

start: we regard independence of outward things as a great good
end: vain and worthless hard to win.
context: The point is not to live with little, but to be able to be content with little, which makes us freer whatever we have.
prompt: What could you happily do without?

start: Plain fare gives as much pleasure as a costly diet
context: Epicurus' own diet was famously simple. Bread and water, eaten when truly hungry, give the deepest pleasure.
prompt: When did a simple thing last give you real pleasure?

start: When we say, then, that pleasure is the end and aim
context: Epicurus corrects the caricature of his teaching. The pleasure he means is the absence of pain and inner trouble.
prompt: What would bring a little more peace to your body and soul today?

start: It is not an unbroken succession of drinking-bouts
context: A pleasant life comes from thinking clearly about what we choose and why, and from letting go of beliefs that disturb us.
prompt: Which of your beliefs causes you the most unrest?

start: Wherefore prudence is a more precious thing even than philosophy
context: For Epicurus, a pleasant life and a good life are the same thing: you cannot have one without the other.
prompt: Where do pleasure and goodness meet in your life?

start: some things happen of necessity, others by chance
context: Against fatalism, Epicurus insists that much of life is up to us. Responsibility depends on it.
prompt: What part of your situation is truly in your own hands?

start: Death is nothing to us; for the body
context: The second of Epicurus' forty core teachings, memorised by his followers. Death cannot harm one who no longer feels.
prompt: What fear might shrink if you looked at it this plainly?

start: The magnitude of pleasure reaches its limit
context: Pleasure has a ceiling: once pain is gone, more does not mean better. This frees us from chasing endless increase.
prompt: Where are you chasing 'more' past the point of enough?

start: Continuous pain does not last long in the flesh
end: does not last for many days together.
context: Epicurus himself suffered from painful illness. His teaching was that severe pain is brief and long pain is bearable.
prompt: What pain have you endured that turned out more bearable than you feared?

start: It is impossible to live a pleasant life without living wisely
context: Pleasure, wisdom and justice are bound together. None can be had fully without the others.
prompt: Which of the three is weakest in your life right now?

start: Some men have sought to become famous and renowned
context: Fame is usually sought for security. Epicurus asks whether it ever really delivers it.
prompt: What are you hoping recognition will give you?

start: No pleasure is in itself evil
context: The problem is never pleasure itself, but what certain pleasures bring along with them.
prompt: Which pleasure brings trouble along with it?

start: When tolerable security against our fellow-men is attained
context: Epicurus advised his followers to 'live unnoticed', valuing a quiet life among friends over public ambition.
prompt: Where could you choose quiet over attention?

start: Fortune but seldom interferes with the wise man
context: Luck affects the outer edges of a life. What matters most is guided by our own reasoning.
prompt: What part of your life is governed by reason rather than luck?

start: The just man enjoys the greatest peace of mind
context: For Epicurus, justice is valuable partly because it lets us sleep at night.
prompt: Is there anything on your conscience disturbing your peace?

start: Unlimited time and limited time afford an equal amount of pleasure
context: A complete life is not measured by its length. Understood rightly, a finite life can be whole.
prompt: What would make your life feel complete, regardless of its length?

start: He who understands the limits of life
context: Knowing how little we truly need frees us from struggles that were never necessary.
prompt: Which of your struggles is for something you don't really need?

start: All such desires as lead to no pain when they remain ungratified
context: A test for any desire: would going without it actually hurt? If not, it can be let go.
prompt: Which desire would cost you nothing to give up?

start: The same conviction which inspires confidence
context: In an uncertain world, nothing makes us more secure than friends.
prompt: Who makes you feel safe, and do you make them feel the same?

start: Of our desires some are natural and necessary
context: Epicurus' famous threefold sorting of desires. An ancient commentator gives examples: drink when thirsty; fine food; crowns and statues in one's honour.
prompt: Sort three of your current desires into these three kinds.

start: On this blissful day, which is also the last of my life
context: Written by Epicurus on the day he died, in great pain. Memories of friendship and conversation outweighed everything else.
prompt: Which conversations would you want to remember at the end?

source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things II
start: The nations wax, the nations wane away
context: Lucretius pictures the generations as relay runners, each handing the torch of life to the next.
prompt: What are you carrying that you hope to hand on?

source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things III
start: And in fee-simple life is given to none
context: Life is lent, not owned. And the eternity after death, Lucretius argues, is no more frightening than the eternity before birth.
prompt: If life is on loan, how do you want to use it?

source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things III
start: The man who sickens of his home goes out
end: guessing not the cause of ail.
context: A strikingly modern portrait of restlessness: the rich man rushing to his country house, bored on arrival, rushing back to town, always fleeing himself.
prompt: What are you running from by keeping busy?

source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things III
start: why not, Even like a banqueter, depart the halls
context: Nature speaks to someone afraid of dying: if your life has been good, why not leave it like a guest who has dined well?
prompt: What would it mean to feel 'laden with life'?

source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things III
start: those tortures said to be In Acheron
context: Lucretius reads the myths of the underworld as pictures of our own anxieties, which we suffer now, not after death.
prompt: Which torment of yours lives only in your mind?

source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things II
start: O wretched minds of men!
context: Lucretius laments how people waste their short lives striving for power, when nature asks only for freedom from pain and a mind at ease.
prompt: What does your nature actually ask of you today?

source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things IV
start: Since from amid the well-spring of delights
context: Even in the middle of pleasure, something bitter rises, often regret or unease of the mind.
prompt: What bitterness rises in you even amid good things?

source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things V
start: But rather this: To look on all things
context: Lucretius contrasts anxious rituals with what he sees as true reverence: looking on the world with calm and clarity.
prompt: What would you see differently if you looked with a mind at peace?

source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things III
start: Therefore death to us Is nothing
context: Lucretius restates Epicurus in verse, at the heart of his long argument against the fear of death.
prompt: How much of your life is shaped by a fear of its ending?
